hook: An FBI-submitted still image captured by a U.S. military sensor system over the Western United States, showing a small dark circular object near a crosshair reticle against an indistinct mountain or cloud background. The operator could not positively identify the object.
why_it_matters: This image represents a rare instance of the FBI formally submitting sensor imagery to AARO as part of the UAP disclosure process, indicating inter-agency reporting pipelines exist between law enforcement and the defense-side anomaly office. The fact that the original imagery was redacted before AARO received it raises questions about what information was withheld even within the government's own disclosure chain. The absence of an accompanying mission report and the corrupted system timestamp compound the analytical gaps, leaving the object unidentified with no contextual metadata to resolve it.

key_findings.finding: The image was captured by a U.S. military sensor system and submitted by the FBI to AARO, demonstrating cross-agency UAP reporting.
The original imagery was altered with redactions prior to submission to AARO, meaning even the government's designated UAP office received an incomplete version of the evidence.
No accompanying mission report was provided, leaving the operational context — including platform, altitude, speed, and mission type — entirely unknown.
The operator who captured the imagery reported being unable to positively identify the UAP, ruling out a straightforward misidentification by the sensor crew.
The date embedded in the image is incorrect due to the system clock not being set, making the precise date of the observation unverifiable from the image itself.

legacy_program_connections.reasoning: The FBI formally submitted this imagery to AARO as part of the UAP reporting pipeline established under the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office mandate.

The image originates from an unspecified U.S. military sensor system, which may connect to military imaging or intelligence infrastructure historically associated with Wright-Patterson, though no direct link is stated.
